fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Hydrogen, Brown's Gas and Expanded Water", "body": "George Wiseman opens by recapping why he treats hydrogen as a macronutrient rather than a micronutrient, noting that it makes up about 62 percent of the body by volume and that gut bacteria normally free it from the food we eat. He then separates Brown's gas from plain molecular hydrogen: roughly 67 percent hydrogen and 33 percent oxygen, plus a third fraction he calls electrically expanded water, which he says forms between the cathode and anode only in machines without the membrane that ordinary hydrogen generators use. In his analogy hydrogen is a pile of bricks, and those extra electrons are the energy that builds the house."}, {"title": "Water That Moves Itself", "body": "George leans on Professor Gerald Pollack's work at the University of Washington on what Pollack calls the fourth phase of water, a slippery, negatively charged exclusion zone gel that forms wherever water meets a water loving surface. George uses it to frame two puzzles he says conventional fluid dynamics leaves open: how blood reaches every fingertip as evenly as the organs beside the heart, and where the pressure to push it through the capillaries comes from. He points to the same capillary action that lifts water up a 300 foot redwood, and Chance compares that pull to current running through a circuit, which George answers by calling us electrical beings."}, {"title": "Answering the Hit Piece on Lye", "body": "Chance raises a YouTube video attacking the AquaCure, and George answers its central fear, the lye. He explains that water on its own will not carry current, so the machine needs a catalyst, and that after years of testing thousands of electrolytes he settled on lye because it stays in the machine, is cheap, is easy to find and works efficiently. He lists its everyday uses, from neutralizing acid in municipal water systems to glazing pretzels, making soap from wood ash, cleaning milk lines on the ranch and producing biodiesel, and recalls being soaked in a 50 percent solution, ten times the concentration the AquaCure uses."}, {"title": "An Inventor's Road to the AquaCure", "body": "George has built electrolyzers since 1986 and first wanted Brown's gas as a welding gas, but the machines he was quoted cost around $300,000, so he built his own, which he says tested twice as efficient at half the size and weight. When cheap Asian welding units arrived he thought he was finished, until the health application appeared. Now he buys those machines and rebuilds each one over about eight hours with almost $300 of extra components, and says 40 grams of lye does the job where the maker recommends 250. A $10,000 manufacturing course waits on a business reorganization, and his stated goal is Brown's gas in every home."}, {"title": "Frequencies, Sludge and a Growing Earth", "body": "George explains that he added a pulse width modulator so users can vary the frequency impressed on the electrolyzer, setting a base of 420 while many people prefer 528, though he is quick to say he is not a frequencies expert for health. Chance ties 528 to his solfeggio tuning fork work and the solar plexus. In his solo outro Chance returns to the sludge electrolysis leaves behind, which he describes as matching the stainless steel plates even though the plates never lose weight, and openly speculates that the sun and moon might act as cathode and anode, and that the Earth may be growing rather than its floodwaters receding."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Inventor George Wiseman returns on hydrogen deficiency, Gerald Pollack's fourth phase of water, and how the AquaCure AC50 differs from a hydrogen generator.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Negative Weirdness and the Healing Crisis", "body": "George explains that some people who start inhaling Brown's gas report headaches, one of them unable to inhale for more than a minute, which puzzled him because he considers the gas pure nutrition. His conclusion is that sometimes healing is uncomfortable, a pattern Chance recognizes from biofield tuning as a healing crisis. George contrasts his own first session in March 2016, after which he lay wide awake all night, with his current wife's first session, which gave her the best night's sleep she could remember, and describes inhaling at the computer to stay alert without coffee."}, {"title": "Keeping the Technology Alive Through Hard Times", "body": "Glad to be speaking somewhere more private, George looks ahead, predicting a financial crisis that leads into food crises. He frames his work as a mission from what he calls God: keeping these technologies alive and spread at the grassroots so they exist on the other side of hard times. Chance asks whether hydrogen as a macronutrient changes how much food a person needs, and George says he now eats one small meal a day, calling the hydrogen from Brown's gas calorie free nutrition. Chance likens it to a different form of biological equity."}, {"title": "Why Results Can Take Months", "body": "Asked what might be missing when someone feels the AquaCure is not helping, George says only about one buyer in a thousand returns it for that reason, and that people who are already healthy will notice little change. He describes his own gradual improvements, with patches of skin peeling away within about three weeks and lost feeling in his hand returning in reverse of the way it faded, his youngest scars healing first. Because this is nutrition rather than drugs, he says, the real payoff is maintenance, and he cites rodent studies showing healthy lifespan gains of 30 and 50 percent in mice."}, {"title": "Strength, Recovery, and the Sideline Pitch", "body": "Chance describes moving from daily gym sessions to lifting three days a week, giving his nervous system a full 48 hours to recover, and asks whether Brown's gas helps recovery and strength. George says his muscles hardened, that in his 60s he could still drop and do 15 push-ups without exercising, that a sprained shoulder he expected to take three weeks healed in three days, and that four hours on a jackhammer left him with no soreness. He wants the Buffalo Bills inhaling on the sideline, and Chance imagines rival teams and their fans copying them."}, {"title": "Water That Remembers", "body": "Chance raises water memory and Veda Austin's freezing experiments, where intention shapes the ice, and George agrees, describing new water condensed from a Brown's gas flame that, sitting in sunlight beside a bottle of 50 mineral supplements, grew a white sludge containing all 50 minerals. He recounts ice forming a W during an intention focused on him, Masaru Emoto's work, Luc Montagnier's DNA frequencies sent by telephone to pure water, and cattle given purified slaughterhouse water showing the stress markers of the slaughtered herd. Both land on gratitude, which George says draws more nourishment from food."}]
